name: Beta-alanine
lead: Beta-alanine is a naturally occurring non-proteinogenic amino acid (3-aminopropanoic acid) that is the rate-limiting precursor of carnosine, a dipeptide stored at high concentration in skeletal muscle, where it helps buffer the acid that builds up during hard exercise.[1][37] Sold as a powder or capsule and built into most pre-workout formulas, it is used by lifters and athletes who want to get through more high-repetition work and hard intervals, which feeds the training volume behind muscle size, conditioning and a leaner, more developed physique.[1][14]

The chain people describe is indirect: more beta-alanine increases muscle carnosine, carnosine buffers hydrogen ions, delayed fatigue lets a person sustain efforts of roughly 0.5 to 10 minutes or complete more repetitions in a set, and more productive training over months supports better physique outcomes.[1][14] Beta-alanine does not itself build muscle tissue; in bodybuilding and looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a performance and training-volume aid, not an anabolic compound.[14] Its best-known acute effect is paraesthesia, a dose-dependent tingling of the skin, particularly the face, neck and hands, which many users recognise as 'the tingles'.[1][14][27]

Meta-analyses of placebo-controlled trials report small average benefits for exercise capacity, with effects concentrated in efforts of about one to four minutes and weaker or less consistent results for very short or very long efforts.[3][4][14] The International Society of Sports Nutrition published a position stand on the supplement in 2015, and later reviews of leading sport supplements include it alongside creatine and caffeine.[7][14]

paras: Beta-alanine is taken by lifters, CrossFit-style athletes, rowers, runners and combat-sport athletes to support high-repetition sets and high-intensity intervals. Trials have tested it in high-intensity functional training, sport climbing, 10-km running time trials, tennis and multi-ingredient pre-workout products.[8][9][10][15][35]

For physique goals, the argument made by users and by some researchers is about training quality: if fatigue sets in later, a person can complete more work in the 8 to 20 repetition range or in conditioning intervals, and sustained volume over weeks is what drives adaptation. The ISSN position stand reported mixed results for strength and body composition, with short studies showing more training volume and lower perceived fatigue and longer studies of 8 to 10 weeks finding no added strength or body-composition benefit over placebo.[14]
Because it does not directly add muscle, its place in looksmaxxing and bodybuilding forums is as an adjunct to training volume rather than an anabolic compound.

A 2023 narrative review assessed carnosine and beta-alanine supplementation in human medicine more broadly.[12] Registered trials have examined beta-alanine in adults with overweight or obesity and prediabetes (NCT05329610) and in cognition during a simulated military operation (NCT04250480).[21][22] The ISSN position stand also described early evidence of benefits for tactical athletes and noted that carnosine's antioxidant and anti-glycation roles are supported mainly by laboratory and animal work.[14]

A 2017 systematic review and meta-analysis of 40 double-blind placebo-controlled studies (1,461 participants) concluded that beta-alanine supplementation has a small overall benefit for exercise measures.[3] A 2024 meta-analysis restricted to trained young men performing maximal or supramaximal efforts of 0.5 to 10 minutes (18 studies, 331 participants) found an overall effect size of 0.39 in favour of beta-alanine, with larger effects in efforts of 4 to 10 minutes.[4]

The ISSN position stand concluded that several weeks of supplementation raises muscle carnosine and improves performance, with the largest benefit in open-ended tasks and time trials lasting one to four minutes, little or no benefit under 60 seconds, modest benefit beyond four minutes and no consistent benefit beyond about 25 minutes. It cited a meta-analysis with a median improvement of 2.85 percent in the 1 to 4 minute range. Several of its authors disclose ties to supplement companies.[14]

Individual studies report varied results. A 23-day randomised trial of 16 men found the beta-alanine group cut their 10-km time by about 169 seconds versus about 54 seconds in the placebo group, with the authors noting its small size, male-only sample and lack of muscle carnosine measurement.[15] Studies of multi-ingredient pre-workout blends containing beta-alanine and caffeine in bench press and basketball tasks cannot isolate beta-alanine from the other ingredients.[8][13]
A 2024 overview of sport supplements covers beta-alanine alongside creatine, nitrates, caffeine and protein, and reviews of nutrition for female athletes have also considered it.[5][7]

The ISSN position stand reported that carnosine rises by up to about 64 percent after four weeks of daily supplementation and up to about 80 percent after ten weeks, with large differences between responders, and that muscle carnosine returns to baseline over roughly 6 to 15 weeks after stopping.[14] Because the benefit is tied to accumulating carnosine over weeks, rather than to a single dose, the stand describes daily intake over several weeks, taken in divided portions or sustained-release form, as the pattern used in studies.[14]

Combinations studied include sodium bicarbonate, which the stand described as likely to give a modest additive effect in efforts limited by acidosis, and creatine, where studies with a beta-alanine-only arm found no clear synergy.[14] Multi-ingredient pre-workouts typically contain a few grams of beta-alanine per serving alongside caffeine and other ingredients.[14][24]

The only consistently reported adverse effect is paraesthesia, a tingling sensation that depends on dose.[1] The ISSN stand describes it as usually affecting the face, neck and hands, as typically fading within 60 to 90 minutes, and as reduced by smaller divided doses or sustained-release forms.[14] Forum participants describe disliking this effect; one T Nation poster said they would prefer a beta-alanine-free version of a drink because of 'the tingles'.[27]

Wikipedia notes that no important adverse effects have been reported but that information on long-term use and on safety in combination with other supplements is lacking, and that many studies did not test supplement purity or for banned substances.[1] The ISSN stand likewise said long-term data beyond one year are lacking.[14] One forum user asked whether chronic supplementation could oversaturate carnosine and slow metabolism, citing a study on glucose uptake; the question was posed on T Nation without a published human study cited in support.[25] A registered trial examined 24 weeks of beta-alanine on muscle taurine and clinical blood parameters in healthy men (NCT03655041).[20]

Carnosine (beta-alanyl-L-histidine) occurs at about 17 to 25 mmol/kg dry muscle and contributes roughly 10 to 20 percent of buffering capacity in type I and II fibres; its imidazole group has a pKa near 6.8, suited to buffering.[1][37] Supplementing carnosine itself is less efficient because it is broken down into histidine and beta-alanine on digestion, so only about 40 percent of its weight is available as beta-alanine.[1] Human studies reported that oral beta-alanine raises muscle carnosine in the vastus lateralis and relates to high-intensity cycling capacity.[18][19]

Carnosine was first described in meat extract by the Russian chemist Vladimir Gulevich and colleagues around 1900, according to Wikipedia, and is also credited with antioxidant, metal-chelating and anti-glycation properties in laboratory work.[37] The ISSN stand estimated carnosine's share of muscle buffering at anywhere from about 7 percent in human data to higher figures in animal data.[14]

Beta-alanine is also a weak agonist at glycine receptors and has been reported to act at GABA-A, GABA-C and NMDA co-agonist sites, leading some authors to call it a putative small-molecule neurotransmitter.[1]

It is formed endogenously from the breakdown of dihydrouracil and carnosine, can be transaminated with pyruvate, and is a component of pantothenic acid (vitamin B5) and so of coenzyme A.[1] A review of histidine metabolism describes the carnosine pathway.[6] The ISSN stand also discussed taurine, noting animal data showing lower circulating taurine but human data showing no meaningful change in muscle taurine.[14]

Industrially it is produced from ammonia and beta-propiolactone according to Wikipedia;[1] Grokipedia describes ammoniation of acrylic acid.[2] Its formula is C3H7NO2 and it lacks a stereocentre.[1][2] It is a water-soluble white crystalline solid.[1]

Beta-alanine appears in many commercial pre-workouts. On T Nation, the site's own products include formulas with 2 g and 3.5 g of beta-alanine per serving, and its marketing describes carnosine increases of up to 58 percent in four weeks and 80 percent in ten weeks.[23][24][26] A product developer on the forum said the company discussed dosing with a beta-alanine researcher and described a cumulative loading approach.[28] Customers discuss out-of-stock products and tingling in the same threads.[29][27]
On looksmax.org the supplement shows up in short threads pairing it with taurine and other amino acids, usually as part of general supplement and training-stack chatter.[38]

Human trials are numerous and mostly small. Meta-analyses: 40 studies in 2017[3] and 18 studies in trained men in 2024.[4] Randomised trials include a 4-week study in high-intensity functional training participants measuring neuromuscular fatigue,[9] a study in sport climbers,[10] an acute pre-workout study in well-trained basketball players,[13] a pre-workout blend versus caffeine bench-press crossover,[8] and a 23-day trial of 10-km running time in active men.[15] Another trial combined nutritional supplementation with aerobic exercise to look at brain systems.[11]

Registered trials cover muscle carnosine (NCT00813553), aerobic-anaerobic transition performance in endurance athletes (NCT05096793), CrossFit performance (NCT05772988), high-intensity interval training (NCT03708185), heart rate response (NCT01745016), tennis players (NCT05427409) and simulated wrestling matches (NCT07641907).[30][31][32][33][34][35][36]

timeline.event: Gulewitsch and Amiradzhibi describe carnosine in meat extract, according to the Wikipedia carnosine article.[37]
A study reports absorption of oral beta-alanine and its effect on carnosine synthesis in human vastus lateralis.[18]
A study links beta-alanine supplementation, muscle carnosine and high-intensity cycling capacity.[19]
International Society of Sports Nutrition position stand on beta-alanine published.[14]
Meta-analysis of 40 trials published in the British Journal of Sports Medicine.[3]
A 23-day trial reports shorter 10-km times in active men taking beta-alanine versus placebo.[15]
A narrative review assesses carnosine and beta-alanine in human medicine.[12]
Meta-analysis in trained young men reports an overall effect size of 0.39.[4]

lore.intro: Beta-alanine is discussed on T Nation mostly as one ingredient in pre-workouts, and 'the tingles' are a recurring topic of both fondness and complaint [27][25].

claims.claim: Beta-alanine raises muscle carnosine and so lets you do more work at high intensity.
claims.believers: Product pages and forum posts state that carnosine rises by up to 58 percent in four weeks and 80 percent in ten weeks, which they say increases work that can be performed at high intensities.[23]
claims.experts: Meta-analyses report small but statistically significant benefits for exercise measures, strongest for efforts of 1 to 10 minutes, and the ISSN stand reports similar carnosine increases.[3][4][14]

claims.claim: The tingling is a sign it is working.
claims.believers: Some users treat the tingles as confirmation that the product is active; others report disliking them.[27]
claims.experts: Paraesthesia is a dose-dependent effect reported in the literature;[1] the ISSN stand notes it is reduced by divided doses without loss of carnosine loading, and the sources do not link its intensity to performance effects.[14]

claims.believers: Marketing for pre-workouts describes sustained power and rapid recovery between sets from beta-alanine.[24][26]
claims.experts: The 2024 trained-male meta-analysis focused on efforts of 0.5 to 10 minutes;[4] the ISSN stand reported little or no benefit under 60 seconds and mixed strength results.[14] A multi-ingredient bench-press study cannot isolate beta-alanine from the other ingredients.[8]

claims.claim: Chronic use could oversaturate carnosine and slow metabolism or cause fatigue.
claims.believers: A forum user raised this after reading a study on carnosine and glucose uptake.[25]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes that long-term safety data are lacking, and the ISSN stand says data beyond one year are lacking; no human study cited here tests carnosine oversaturation.[1][14]

claims.claim: Loading over weeks matters more than a single pre-workout dose.
claims.believers: A product developer described a cumulative loading process measured in grams over several weeks.[28]
claims.experts: The ISSN stand reports muscle carnosine rising over weeks, with single large doses causing strong tingling and not loading muscle effectively; the 2024 analysis found significant effects at four weeks.[4][14]

claims.claim: Beta-alanine builds muscle and improves physique directly.
claims.believers: Some pre-workout marketing lumps it with muscle-building ingredients.[24]
claims.experts: The ISSN stand reported no added strength or body-composition benefit in 8 to 10 week studies, and Wikipedia describes the mechanism as buffering that delays fatigue.[1][14]

claims.claim: Taking it with creatine or sodium bicarbonate gives extra benefit.
claims.believers: Multi-ingredient stacks combine beta-alanine with creatine and caffeine.[24]
claims.experts: The ISSN stand described likely modest additive effects with sodium bicarbonate in acidosis-limited efforts and no clear synergy with creatine in studies that had a beta-alanine-only arm.[14]
